how-to-split-tests-across-ci-shards.html.text:
← CI Test Shard Balancer

How to split tests across CI shards evenly

If one of your parallel CI jobs always finishes last while the others sit idle, the split is by count, not by time. Here is how to split by measured duration, and how to decide how many shards are worth paying for.

1. Get per-test timings as JUnit XML

Every mainstream runner can write JUnit XML with a time on each test case. Run the whole suite once, on one machine, with it switched on:

pytest --junitxml=junit.xml
JEST_JUNIT_ADD_FILE_ATTRIBUTE=true jest --reporters=default --reporters=jest-junit
gotestsum --junitfile junit.xml ./...
mvn test            # reports in target/surefire-reports/TEST-*.xml
gradle test         # reports in build/test-results/test/*.xml
bundle exec rspec --format RspecJunitFormatter --out junit.xml

For Jest, the file attribute matters: without it the report has test names but no file path, and a shard command needs file paths. Option names are from each project's own documentation as best understood when this page was written; check them against your versions.

2. Balance by duration, not by count

Splitting 24 files into four groups of six looks fair, but if one file takes ninety seconds and most take five, the group holding it is slow. Putting tests on shards so the slowest shard is as short as possible is the multiway number-partitioning problem. It is hard to solve exactly in general, but a simple rule gets close: take the longest file, put it on the least-loaded shard, repeat. That is the LPT rule, and it is never worse than about a third above the best possible split. A pass of moving and swapping files between shards then evens out what is left, and for small suites the best split can be found exactly.

The CI Test Shard Balancer does all of that from the XML in your browser, and prints the file list for each shard.

3. Look for the test that cannot be split

Total time divided by the number of shards is the ideal shard. If one file takes longer than that, it sets the floor: no split can finish before it does, however many shards you add. The tool flags these. If the file holds many tests, group by single test instead; if it is one long test, that test is the thing to speed up or split.

4. Pick the number of shards from setup time

Every shard job pays a fixed cost before its first test: checkout, dependency restore, build. With 60 seconds of setup and a 10-minute suite, going from 4 to 8 shards cuts the test part from 2.5 minutes to 1.25 but adds four more setups. Wall-clock time is the slowest shard plus setup, and billed time is roughly shards times that, so there is a shard count past which you pay more and wait about the same. Enter your setup seconds and an optional wall-clock target and the tool prices every count in a table.

5. Put it in CI, and keep it fresh

Paste the emitted commands, or use the GitHub Actions matrix JSON with fromJSON in a job's strategy.matrix. Timings drift as tests are added, so recompute every few weeks, or let CI tell you:

node cli.mjs split junit.xml --shards 4 --max-imbalance-pct 20

That exits 1 when the slowest shard is more than 20 percent over an even share. Timings also vary from run to run, so treat the result as a good starting point rather than a promise. If you want a split that adapts during every run, a paid service does that; see the comparison.

Flaky tests distort timings because reruns inflate them. Rule those out with the Flaky Test Finder first.

Common questions

Why is one of my CI shards always the slowest?

Most simple splits give each shard the same number of test files in alphabetical or hashed order. Test files differ a lot in duration, so shards with the slow files finish last and the others sit idle. Balancing by measured duration fixes that part; a single very slow file can still set the floor.

Do more shards always make CI faster?

No. Each shard pays a fixed setup cost, and wall-clock time can never go below the longest single test or file plus setup. Past that point more shards only add billed minutes.

How often should I recompute the split?

Whenever the suite changes a lot, and otherwise every few weeks. A CI step that runs the CLI with --max-imbalance-pct tells you when the split has drifted.

Split your tests into evenly timed CI shards

Paste the JUnit XML your test runner already writes. See how long your slowest shard is now, how long it could be, how many shards are worth paying for, and the exact test files to put on each shard.

Nothing is uploaded. The report is read in this browser and never leaves your device. It is a heuristic over the timings you give it; real runs vary.

1. Load your timings

Works with pytest (--junitxml), Jest (jest-junit), Go (gotestsum --junitfile), Maven/Gradle and RSpec (rspec_junit_formatter).

Setup seconds is the fixed cost every shard job pays before its first test (checkout, install, cache restore). It is why adding shards stops paying off. “One report per current shard” needs several reports, one from each shard you run today.

2. What changes

Billed minutes = N × (slowest shard + setup), the conservative model. Shards that finish early are billed for less in practice, and your CI provider may round each job up to a whole minute.

Paste into your pipeline


  


  

    
Run it in CI

    
Same engine, zero dependencies, one file. Fails the job when your current split drifts away from an even one, so it does not quietly decay as tests are added:

    
node cli.mjs split junit.xml --shards 4 --setup-seconds 60
node cli.mjs split shard-*.xml --current-from-reports     # each file = one shard you run today
node cli.mjs split junit.xml --shards 6 --group test --matrix   # GitHub Actions matrix JSON
node cli.mjs split junit.xml --shards 4 --max-imbalance-pct 20   # exit 1 if unbalanced

    
Get cli.mjs and engine.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call, ever. Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 over the imbalance limit, 2 unreadable file or bad option.

  


  

    
Common questions

    
How do I split tests evenly across CI shards?

    
Export per-test timings as JUnit XML from a recent run, paste them here, and choose the number of shards. The page treats it as a multiway number-partitioning problem: it places the longest files first on the least-loaded shard, then improves the result by moving and swapping files between shards, and for small suites it searches for the exact optimum. It prints the files for each shard as a runnable command.

    
Which test reports does it read?

    
JUnit XML from pytest (--junitxml), Jest through jest-junit, Go through gotestsum or go-junit-report, Maven Surefire and Gradle, and RSpec through rspec_junit_formatter. The format is detected automatically and can be forced.

    
Why is my slowest shard still slow after balancing?

    
One test or file may be longer than an even share of the whole suite. It cannot be split across shards, so it sets the floor on wall-clock time no matter how many shards you add. The page flags any such unit and, if you grouped by file, suggests grouping by test instead.

    
How many shards should I use?

    
Enter your fixed setup time per shard (checkout, dependency install) and an optional wall-clock target. The page sweeps shard counts, shows slowest shard, wall-clock and billed minutes for each, and suggests the cheapest count that meets the target. Setup time is why more shards stop paying off.

    
Is my test report uploaded anywhere?

    
No. The page reads what you paste or load in your browser and makes no network request. The CLI reads local files and makes no network call. There is no model and no randomness, so the same input always gives the same split.

    
Are the predicted times a guarantee?

    
No. Test timings vary from run to run and with the machine, so real shards will differ from the prediction. Treat the split as a good starting point and re-run the tool on fresh timings every few weeks.

vs-knapsack-pro.html.text:
← CI Test Shard Balancer

This tool vs. Knapsack Pro

Different jobs. Knapsack Pro is a paid service that keeps splitting your tests for you on every run. This is a free calculator that gives you one balanced split, today, from timing reports you already have.

What each one is for

Knapsack Pro is a commercial service for splitting a test suite across parallel CI nodes. Its public documentation describes recording timing data from your CI runs and a dynamic “queue mode” that gives tests to nodes as they become free, with libraries for several test frameworks. It is a subscription product; see its own pricing page for current plans.

This tool reads JUnit XML you already have (pytest, Jest, Go, Maven/Gradle, RSpec), computes a fixed split into N shards, and prints the files for each shard, a GitHub Actions matrix, and a sweep of shard counts priced against your setup time. It keeps no history, has no account, and sends nothing anywhere.

QuestionThis toolKnapsack Pro
CostFree, MIT licencePaid subscription; check its pricing page
Account or signupNoneRequired, with an API token in your CI
Where your test names and timings goNowhere; processed in your browser or on your machineSent to its service so it can record timings (per its documentation)
Split adapts during a runNo. A fixed split; recompute it when timings changeYes, in queue mode, tests are handed out as nodes free up
Timing historyNone. You supply a recent JUnit reportRecorded automatically from your runs
Absorbs a slow node or a one-off slow testNoLargely yes, because work is assigned late
How many shards are worth paying forYes: a sweep priced with your setup seconds and an optional wall-clock targetNot its stated focus

CI gate when a split has driftedYes: --max-imbalance-pct exits 1Not applicable; it re-splits on its own

Use this tool when you want a good split now without an account, your timings are stable enough that a split holds for a few weeks, you cannot send test data to a third party, or you first want to know whether more shards would even help. Use Knapsack Pro when run-to-run variation is large, you do not want to maintain a split, or you want splitting that adapts during a run. Plenty of teams could start with the free calculation and move to a service if variation proves to be the problem.

Statements about Knapsack Pro summarise its public documentation as best understood when this page was written and may be out of date. Check its documentation for the current feature set and pricing.

Common questions

Is CI Test Shard Balancer a replacement for Knapsack Pro?

For one narrow job, yes: if you can live with a fixed split that you recompute from fresh JUnit XML every few weeks, this tool gives you balanced file lists and a GitHub Actions matrix for free, with no account. It is not a replacement if you want splitting that adapts on every run.

Where does Knapsack Pro do better?

Knapsack Pro describes a dynamic queue mode in which tests are handed to CI nodes as they become free, so a slow node or an unexpected slow test is absorbed during that very run, and it records timing data from your runs automatically. A fixed split computed beforehand cannot react to variation inside a run, and this tool keeps no history. If run-to-run variation is large, or you do not want to maintain a split, the paid service is the better fit.

Why would I use the free tool instead?

When you want a split now, from reports you already have, without signing up or sending test names and timings to a third party; when your timings are stable enough that a fixed split holds; or when you want a CI gate that tells you the current split has drifted. It also answers how many shards are worth paying for, given your setup time.
